chunks: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Every lapse in the salat is dropped from it, except that God the Exalted completes it with the voluntary prayers. The first thing the servant will be reckoned for is the salat; if it is accepted, what is besides it will be accepted.
The salat, when it is raised during the beginning of its prescribed time, returns to its owner and it is white, shining, saying: 'You preserved me, may God protect you.'
And when it is raised outside its prescribed time, without its proper limits, it returns to its owner and it is black, dark, saying: 'You wasted me, may God waste you.'

key_terms.النَّوَافِلُ: Voluntary/supererogatory prayers that supplement the obligatory salat
key_terms.الْمُحَاسَبَةُ: Divine reckoning/accounting on the Day of Judgment
key_terms.حُدُودُ الصَّلَاةِ: The proper limits and conditions of salat — its time, form, and prerequisites
key_terms.سَهْوٌ: Lapse/forgetfulness in prayer — unintentional errors or shortcomings in performance

ai.seo_question: What happens to a Muslim's prayer on the Day of Judgment according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) teaches Abu Basir about the supreme importance of salat: minor lapses are forgiven through voluntary prayers, but the salat itself is the first and most critical act of worship to be judged on the Day of Resurrection. Using vivid imagery—the prayer returning white and radiant or black and dark—the Imam communicates the spiritual consequences of performing salat on time versus neglecting it. This teaching was addressed to early Shia Muslims who understood salat not merely as a ritual but as a living entity whose spiritual state directly reflects the worshipper's sincerity.
